Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-02
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Recording id: ff-20250602-0423
Attendees: Lina Perez (Redwood AE), Samir Khatri (Redwood SE), Maria Chen (Arcadia, Sr ML Eng), Tom Ortega (Arcadia, Infra), Ravi Singh (Arcadia, CTO)

[00:00] Lina Perez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Lina from Redwood, I'm the AE, and Samir our SE will take most of the deep dive, quick intro round?
[00:08] Maria Chen: Maria here, senior ML eng at Arcadia. We're looking to push a high-throughput assistant in front of triage flows.
[00:13] Tom Ortega: Tom infra, focused on on-prem compliance and network egress.
[00:17] Ravi Singh: Ravi, CTO, listening for architecture/timeframe.
[00:20] Samir Khatri: Great, thanks. Our objective today is to walk through continuous batching internals, scheduler knobs you can tune (max_num_seqs, batch timeout, token caps), KV cache behavior on warm and edge cases, and quantization tradeoffs for your on-prem 4xA100 footprint. I'll call out where dedicated vs hosted differs.

[02:05] Samir Khatri: Quick note before we start—some terms we'll use: "max_num_seqs" = per-GPU active sequence cap the scheduler uses to build minibatches; "batch_timeout_ms" / "queue_timeout_ms" are how long the scheduler will wait to assemble more tokens; "continuous batching" is our running packer that keeps kernels fed by reusing slots across requests.
[03:10] Maria Chen: Can you explain how max_num_seqs interacts with variable length prompts? Our prompts vary a lot, from 10 tokens to 1.2k.
[03:27] Samir Khatri: Sure. If prompts are variable, packing efficiency drops if you set max_num_seqs too high because a single long sequence can pad short ones. You can either set max_num_seqs lower so batches are more homogeneous, or enable per-batch length bucketing. For example, in our internal runs we got better tokens/sec with max_num_seqs=64 and aggressive bucketing vs naive 128 for the same traffic. That said, very long tails (1k+) you want to cap with token_limit to avoid blocking the scheduler.
[04:50] Tom Ortega: Token limit—so that's server-side truncation? We can't lose clinical context.
[04:56] Samir Khatri: Right, token limits can be soft or hard. We generally recommend soft limits with a pre-check in your app—reject or route to a lower-latency path if exceed. For critical clinical prompts, you can pin those to a dedicated pool with higher max_seq or run in dedicated mode with lower multiplexing to preserve context.
[06:12] Maria Chen: How does KV cache warmup look for repeated sessions? Our flows are session-y, so reuse should be big.
[06:25] Samir Khatri: KV cache warmup is huge for cost and latency. If you have many short continuations, prefix/KV caching can avoid recomputation. Caveats: cache indexing is per-session key; when you shard across GPUs or nodes in on-prem, cache misses increase. For private deployments we recommend sticky routing by session id to keep the KV cache hot on the same GPU.
[07:40] Ravi Singh: Sticky routing—does that conflict with load balancing? For our infra we want even GPU utilization.
[07:48] Samir Khatri: There's a tradeoff. Sticky routing increases hit-rate and reduces tokens/recompute, but can lead to imbalance. Our scheduler supports hybrid policies: prefer hot-slot if utilization > threshold else reassign. Also you can set an eviction policy—LRU or TTL—for KV entries so cache growth is bounded.
[09:02] Maria Chen: Any numbers on how much throughput gain?
[09:08] Samir Khatri: In our sim for session-heavy workloads, enabling prefix caching and sticky routing gave ~1.8x tokens/sec for average prompt lengths ~40 tokens and continuation lengths ~20. For doc-long continuations the benefit is higher. If you instead look at p99 latency it's improved because we avoid redundant attention compute.
[10:30] Tom Ortega: What about memory pressure—KV cache size per GPU? We have 80GB A100s but want headroom for other models.
[10:40] Samir Khatri: KV cache is proportional to number of cached tokens * batch size * hidden dims. For a 1B-parameter style model it's smaller, for 13B+ it grows. We expose a config kv_cache_max_tokens and per-session cap. You can also choose to shard KV across GPUs (multi-GPU cache) at cost of cross-device comms. For on-prem low-latency you usually keep KV local.
[12:01] Maria Chen: Let's talk continuous batching scheduler knobs. Which knobs should be first-line for us?
[12:12] Samir Khatri: Start with: 1) max_num_seqs, 2) batch_timeout_ms, 3) token_limit_per_batch, 4) pack_by_length (true/false), 5) slot_reuse_window. Practical tuning path: run with conservative defaults (max_num_seqs=64, batch_timeout_ms=10), measure tokens/sec and p50/p95 lat. Then iterate: if tails high, decrease batch_timeout_ms or lower max_num_seqs; if throughput low but latency fine, increase max_num_seqs.
[13:40] Maria Chen: How do we measure packing efficiency?
[13:45] Samir Khatri: We publish metrics token_packing_ratio and wasted_pad_tokens in Console. For quick bench, sample 10k requests, compute sum(actual_tokens)/sum(padded_tokens). You want that ratio close to 1.0.
[14:30] Tom Ortega: We will share real traffic traces. How sensitive are these knobs to traffic shift? We expect usage spikes during morning triage.
[14:40] Samir Khatri: Traffic shift affects queueing—higher spike will increase batch formation rate and maybe reduce pad overhead. We recommend autoscaling policies tied to queue_length and tokens_per_sec, not just GPU utilization. For on-prem you can configure burst pools or pre-warm slots.
[16:05] Maria Chen: Quantization—we plan q4_0 or int8. What's the typical throughput/latency difference vs fp16?
[16:16] Samir Khatri: Roughly speaking, q4_0 gets ~1.6-2x tokens/sec over fp16 on same hardware with minimal model quality degradation for many workloads. int8 can give higher gains but sometimes has more quality delta. For the scheduler, quantization reduces kernel time but can change token-generation variance which affects packing; we recommend re-benchmarking packing ratios after quantization.
[17:40] Ravi Singh: Any gotchas for on-prem with quant and MKL/CUDA?
[17:46] Samir Khatri: Watch for kernel compatibility; our runtime will choose compiled kernels per quant mode. On older driver stacks you may need a rebuild. Also caloric note—quantized kernels sometimes use different tensor core paths, watch for NUMA placement and PCI lanes for multi-GPU sync.
[19:22] Maria Chen: You mentioned token limits earlier—how to handle long outputs like report generations where tokens could be 2k+?
[19:31] Samir Khatri: For long outputs we recommend streaming or chunked generation, and treat long-running streams with a different scheduling profile: lower multiplexing and larger max_num_seqs reserved, or pin to dedicated machines. Also you can do hierarchical generation: extract/plan stages on smaller models and final render on the large one.
[21:05] Tom Ortega: About scheduler holes—what is slot_reuse_window?
[21:12] Samir Khatri: slot_reuse_window is how long an idle GPU slot is kept warm for quick re-attach. Short windows reduce memory overhead but increase cache churn; longer windows increase hit rates but keep memory reserved. For sessiony workloads, set longer window (e.g., 30s-2min).
[22:30] Maria Chen: We use a mix of short chats and a minority of long report jobs. What are sane defaults?
[22:40] Samir Khatri: Use two pools: a high-qps pool (max_num_seqs 64, batch_timeout_ms 5, slot_reuse_window 30s, aggressive prefix caching) and a long-job pool (max_num_seqs 8-16, token_limit 4k, batch_timeout_ms 50, dedicated capacity). Route by request type.
[24:10] Ravi Singh: On the networking side, for VPC deployments we worry about session stickiness and LB config—any docs?
[24:18] Lina Perez: I can share our private deployment checklist and VPC LB config examples after the call; they'll include sticky cookie guidance and SNI config for mTLS.
[24:38] Tom Ortega: Great. For the benchmarking, we want to see p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec; also CPU usage and PCIe bandwidth.
[24:49] Samir Khatri: We'll capture those. Our benchmark template includes GPU SM utilization, HBM usage, PCIe rx/tx, kernel times, and scheduler histograms. I'll populate the Arcadia sheet.
[26:00] Maria Chen: Can you talk about continuous batching's behavior at very low qps, like <1 rps per GPU?
[26:08] Samir Khatri: At low qps batching will naturally drop to single-sequence work and batching gains disappear. To optimize latency you can reduce batch_timeout_ms to near-zero and use smaller max_num_seqs or even run in low-multiplex dedicated mode. There's an economic tradeoff—higher latency SLOs at very low qps when multiplexed.
[27:28] Maria Chen: Is there tooling to simulate my production profile?
[27:33] Samir Khatri: Yes, we have a loadgen harness; you can feed the real trace you export and it will run a faithful sim including session stickiness and KV warmups. Use that to prototype knob changes before on-prem runs.
[28:50] Tom Ortega: For on-prem, we will have limited node count. Can Redwood runtime do NUMA-aware placement?
[28:58] Samir Khatri: Yes, runtime respects NUMA topology; we have config flags for strict NUMA placement and PCIe affinity. For dense deployments we recommend pinning GPU processes to CPU cores and isolating network threads to avoid jitter.
[30:12] Maria Chen: Any examples where max_num_seqs backfired?
[30:18] Samir Khatri: A customer set max_num_seqs very high to chase throughput but had a long-tail of 2k token prompts causing all batches to pad and throughput collapsed; tail latency exploded. Their cost went up because they were doing compute on padded tokens. We helped them implement bucketing and a separate long-job pool.
[31:40] Maria Chen: Can we dynamically change max_num_seqs without restarting?
[31:44] Samir Khatri: You can update some scheduler knobs live; others require a soft drain of workers to reinitialize compile profiles. In Redwood Dedicated we support rolling config updates. For private on-prem some flags are hot-reloadable, others not—depends on whether it affects kernel compilation paths.
[33:10] Ravi Singh: We're interested in model compilation; does changing quantization require a full recompilation?
[33:16] Samir Khatri: Often yes. Quant modes can select different kernels; our platform keeps precompiled variants for common quant modes (fp16, q4_0, int8) and can switch fast if variants exist. If you have a custom quant build you may need a compile step.
[34:40] Maria Chen: How do cache eviction and session TTL interact with privacy requirements? We need to ensure patient data is not kept beyond policy.
[34:50] Samir Khatri: You can configure KV cache TTLs to match retention policy and enable automatic purge on session end. For sensitive PII we recommend not caching at all or using encrypted entries with KMS-wrapped keys and audit logs. We'll include config examples in the security pack.
[36:10] Tom Ortega: When you talk about packing efficiency, what about heterogeneous model families? We might run a 7B for quick tasks and 70B for summaries.
[36:20] Samir Khatri: Separate model pools. Continuous batching does not pack across different model binaries. We'll route small tasks to smaller models and keep large models in separate dedicated pools. That avoids wasted memory and mispack.
[37:30] Maria Chen: Do you support multi-tenant isolation on the same cluster for strong SLA?
[37:38] Samir Khatri: Yes, with namespaces and hard resource quotas. For stronger isolation use Dedicated capacity. For private clusters you can combine cgroups and GPU partitioning (MIG where supported) to enforce limits.
[39:00] Maria Chen: Let's dig into a concrete run. Samir, what will you test for our 4xA100 PoC?
[39:06] Samir Khatri: Plan: 1) Baseline with fp16, max_num_seqs 64, batch_timeout_ms 10; 2) Sweep max_num_seqs [32,64,128], batch_timeout_ms [5,10,20], token_limit [512,1024,2048]; 3) Run quant variants q4_0 and int8; 4) KV cache on vs off with sticky routing and TTLs; capture tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99, packing ratio, HBM usage. I will populate the sheet with CSVs for each run.
[40:25] Maria Chen: Will you simulate session stickiness?
[40:28] Samir Khatri: Yes, we'll replay your trace with session ids and hotspot patterns.
[41:10] Tom Ortega: For the on-prem plan, what about KMS integration and key rotation?
[41:16] Lina Perez: We'll include KMS integration notes. For rotation we support HSM/KMS flows and zero-downtime rotation patterns in our private doc.
[42:05] Ravi Singh: How long before we can get a pilot running?
[42:10] Lina Perez: If we sign a pilot contract, we can schedule an infra kickoff and have an image ready in 1-2 weeks, then run smoke benches. Real PoC with data and traffic usually 3-4 weeks.
[43:00] Maria Chen: One more on scheduler telemetry—what dashboards are available?
[43:06] Samir Khatri: Console shows per-route tokens/sec, packing ratio, scheduler queue histograms, per-device HBM, and a kernel latency waterfall. We'll share screenshots and a dashboard export.
[44:20] Tom Ortega: Any notes on PCIe saturation when KV is remote?
[44:28] Samir Khatri: Remote KV means cross-device comms; PCIe can saturate on heavy KV traffic. Prefer local KV or ensure NVLink for multi-GPU servers. We'll measure PCIe tx/rx as part of the benchmark.
[45:40] Maria Chen: Are there quick rules of thumb?
[45:44] Samir Khatri: Yep: keep common path short (short prompts) in high-qps pools, reserve dedicated capacity for long-running heavy jobs, use sticky routing for sessiony workloads, prefer q4_0 for broad use, and always benchmark packing after any change.
[46:55] Ravi Singh: Let's capture the decision points: we want to start pilot with q4_0, two pools, sticky routing, and bench max_num_seqs sweep.
[47:05] Lina Perez: Noted. I'll include that in next steps.
[48:00] Maria Chen: One operational thing—what's the behavior during autoscaler events? If nodes go away what happens to KV?
[48:08] Samir Khatri: Cache is per-node; when a node is drained, its cache is lost. We have an optional spill-to-disk for warm-up but it's slower. Best practice: cordon nodes during maintenance and drain gracefully or rely on our rolling scaling that respects session stickiness.
[49:30] Tom Ortega: Any instructions for reproducible benchmarks?
[49:36] Samir Khatri: We have a benchmarking cookbook. Steps: 1) freeze model/quant, 2) warm KV cache with 10k sessions, 3) replay traffic at target qps, 4) collect metrics for 30-60 minutes, 5) analyze packing_ratio and pad_waste. We'll attach the cookbook.
[51:00] Maria Chen: Can you email the benchmark sheet link now?
[51:05] Samir Khatri: I'll share after the call: https://redwood-internal/benchmarks/arcadia-2025-06 (demo link, will send ACL'd copy).
[51:40] Lina Perez: Recap — Samir runs sweep, Maria shares prompt set and traffic trace, Lina sends pricing/docs and schedules pilot kickoff. Any other items?
[51:54] Ravi Singh: None from me.
[52:00] Tom Ortega: No. Thanks.
[52:05] Maria Chen: Thanks, really helpful.
